title: QuEra Joins $12 Million DOE Project on AI-Designed Quantum Error Correction
html:
Insider Brief

  • QuEra Computing has joined a Harvard-led, $12 million U.S. Department of Energy project to develop AI-designed error correction systems for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
  • The ASQC project will use AI models to identify errors affecting specific scientific workloads and develop tailored error-correcting codes and decoders for applications in chemistry, materials science, quantum simulation and nuclear science.
  • Researchers will test the resulting systems on QuEra‘s neutral-atom quantum computers and hardware at Harvard and MIT, building on earlier work in AI-assisted decoding and quantum circuit design.

PRESS RELEASE — QuEra Computing, the leader in fault-tolerant quantum computing, today announced that it is a collaborating partner in ASQC (Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing), a Harvard-led project that received $12 million from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). ASQC is one of 12 Phase II awards DOE announced on October 9, 2026 under the Genesis Mission, and it will use AI to design error correction matched to the scientific problems DOE cares about, with the goal of bringing useful fault-tolerant quantum computation sooner.

The project brings together multiple organizations including Los Alamos National Laboratory; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; Sandia National Laboratories. Harvard, MIT, Cornell University, NVIDIA, Anthropic and QuEra Computing.

The Genesis Mission, launched in November 2025, aims to integrate the nation’s supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research. The Phase II awards are administered by DOE’s Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) division. Harvard announced ASQC’s project details on November 20, 2026, in the Harvard Gazette.

Error correction is what separates today’s quantum machines from fault-tolerant ones, and the number of physical qubits and operations it consumes largely sets how soon a machine can do useful work. ASQC takes aim at that overhead by tailoring error correction to specific scientific workloads, rather than treating every error and every application the same way.

What ASQC Will Build

  • Train AI models to find the errors that matter most. The models will learn which errors have the greatest effect on specific DOE science problems, including quantum simulation, materials science, chemistry and nuclear science.
  • Use AI to design codes and decoders. Error-correcting codes and the decoders that interpret them will be tailored to those problems.
  • Assemble an AI-driven error correction system. The goal is a fault-tolerant quantum error correction system that can adapt to DOE scientific workloads.
  • Test on real hardware. Results will be tested on QuEra‘s neutral-atom systems and on lab systems at Harvard and MIT.

A Team Built on Published Results

The principal investigator is Mikhail Lukin, Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor at Harvard and co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative, who is also QuEra‘s co-founder and Chief Science Officer. The team includes Markus Greiner (QuEra’s co-founder) and Susanne Yelin (Harvard); Vladan Vuletić (QuEra co-founder and CTO), Soonwon Choi and Harry Zhou (MIT); Eun-Ah Kim (Cornell); researchers from Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley and Sandia national laboratories; Nathan Gemelke and Michael Gullans (QuEra); Krysta Svore (NVIDIA); and Alek Kemeny (Anthropic).

The project builds on earlier work from the team. Previously published results suppressed errors enough that adding qubits reduced logical errors (errors in an error-corrected qubit built from many atoms) rather than increasing them. An April 2026 preprint by Lukin, Yelin and colleagues described a neural-network decoder that reduced error rates by up to 17x compared with existing decoders and ran thousands of times faster. Recent work with QuEra and Anthropic also used large language models to discover state-of-the-art quantum circuits for chemistry, optimization, simulation, numerical computation and number theory. In August 2026, QuEra reported that Anthropic’s Claude, working through Anthropic’s Model Hardware Standard research preview, developed control software that recovered a drifted laser lock in 695 of 700 trials on a dedicated testbed, typically in seconds rather than the minutes an expert needs.

In Harvard’s announcement, Prof. Lukin described the aim of the project: “This is really an attempt to establish scientific foundations for useful fault-tolerant quantum computers.”

Why It Matters for QuEra’s Path to Fault Tolerance

QuEra is building fault-tolerant quantum computers for real world, high-value use cases, from elements already demonstrated in peer-reviewed research. Libra, QuEra’s fault-tolerant system, is planned for Amazon Braket, from AWS, in early 2028. Co-design of error correction with applications, in which QuEra works on the application and the hardware together, supports that roadmap directly and has the potential to accelerate that roadmap: the less overhead error correction requires, the more useful work a fault-tolerant quantum computer can do.

“Error correction overhead decides how soon fault-tolerant machines can start doing useful work. Designing codes and decoders around the problems scientists actually need to solve is a direct way to lower that overhead, and it strengthens and has the potential to accelerate the path we are building toward Libra and our successor Gigaquop quantum computer on AWS,” said Andy Ory, CEO of QuEra Computing.

The project also fits the environment the Genesis Mission describes, in which supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems work together. QuEra designs its systems for existing HPC and data-center environments, with QuEra Gemini deployed on premises since 2025 and QuEra Aquila available on Amazon Braket since 2022.

“Hardware testing is where a design meets reality. We will work with our Harvard and MIT colleagues to run AI-designed codes and decoders on our neutral-atom systems, so the results reflect how real machines behave,” said Nathan Gemelke, co-founder and Chief Technology Strategist at QuEra Computing.

MENTIONED IN THE ARTICLE

QuEra Computing uses research on neutral atoms, developed at Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as the basis for a scalable, programmable quantum computer solution. QuEra’s quantum processing technology is based on trapping, energizing, and shuttling atoms with laser beams.

Harvard University, located in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is a private Ivy League research institution. Established in 1636 under the name Harvard College and in honor of its initial supporter, clergyman John Harvard, it holds the distinction of being the oldest higher education institution in the United States. Its global reputation, financial resources, and rankings have positioned it as one of the world's most esteemed universities.

The United States Department of Energy is a cabinet-level department of the United States Government concerned with the United States' policies regarding energy and safety in handling nuclear material.
